title: Past time
subtitle: Past simple and continuous, past perfect, would, used to, be used to and get used to

rows.use: Single completed actions
rows.example: Sony and Philips **unveiled** the compact disc in 1982.

rows.use: Repeated or habitual actions in the past
rows.example: We **moved** house a lot when I was a child.

rows.use: General truths about the past
rows.example: Early mechanical clocks **were** usually unreliable.

rows.use: Permanent situations and states in the past
rows.example: **Did** the Minoans **have** more sophisticated plumbing than later civilisations?

rows.use: The main events in a story
rows.example: Frank **switched** on the set and **sat** down on the sofa.

rows.use: The present in conditional sentences
rows.example: If we **didn't have** computing, what would the world be like?

rows.use: The present after wish, it's time, would rather, etc.
rows.example: I'd rather Michael **didn't waste** so many evenings on video games.

rows.use: To emphasise contrast in the past
rows.example: Perhaps our grandparents didn't have e-mail, but they **did have** the telephone and telegrams.

rows.use: To emphasise strong feeling in the past
rows.example: I **did enjoy** our visit to the Science Museum last summer.

theory.title: Past simple vs present perfect simple

blocks.text: In general, the **past simple** is used to refer to periods of time or moments which are **finished**. The **present perfect** is used to refer to periods of time which **continue up to the present**.

blocks.correct: The nineteenth century **saw** many technological advances, such as the camera and the electric light bulb.
blocks.incorrect: The nineteenth century **has seen** many technological advances, such as the camera and the electric light bulb.

blocks.correct: There **have been** many technological advances in recent years, the most important being the spread of the Internet.
blocks.incorrect: There **were** many technological advances in recent years, the most important being the spread of the Internet.

blocks.intro: The past simple is used to refer to events at a specific time in the past. The present perfect is used when the specific time something happened isn't important or relevant, or when the present result of a past event is important.
items: I **sent** my first e-mail six months ago.

rows.use: Actions in progress at a particular moment in the past
rows.example: **Were** you **chatting** to Matt online at midnight last night?

rows.use: Actions in progress around a particular moment in the past
rows.example: At the turn of the twentieth century, many discoveries **were being made** in physics and other sciences.

rows.use: Temporary situations and series of actions in the past
rows.example: At the time, I **was working** for a large software company in California.

rows.use: Changing and developing situations in the past
rows.example: I **was getting** frustrated with my internet provider so I decided to change.

rows.use: Annoying or amusing past habits (usually with always)
rows.example: When she was young, Tina **was always taking** things apart to see how they worked.

rows.use: Background information in a story
rows.example: It **was raining** outside and people **were making** their way home after work.

rows.use: Actions in progress over a period of time
rows.example: **Were** you **writing** e-mails all yesterday morning?

rows.use: Two actions in progress at the same time
rows.example: While I **was playing** a computer game, my brother **was doing** his homework.

rows.use: The present and the future after wish, it's time, would rather, etc.
rows.example: I wish we **were going** to the computer fair next weekend.

items: We often use the past continuous to describe **background** events in progress and the past simple for the **main** events: We **were talking** about MP3s when Andrea **mentioned** her new music website.
We normally use the past simple to describe **regular or repeated** actions in the past, not the past continuous: When I was a child, I **visited** my grandmother every week.

blocks.intro: Past continuous vs present perfect continuous
items: In general, the past continuous is used to refer to actions in progress during periods of time or at moments which are **finished**. The present perfect continuous is used to refer to actions in progress during periods of time which **continue up to the present**.
We **were working** on my computer for four hours yesterday.
We **have been working** on my computer for four hours so far.

rows.use: Situations and states before the past
rows.example: **Had** you **had** your computer long before it broke down?

rows.use: Completed actions before a moment in the past
rows.example: When talking films appeared, the cinema **had already become** a popular form of entertainment.

rows.use: A series of actions continuing up to a moment in the past
rows.example: When Dimitra called, I **had managed** to fix her computer.

rows.use: Completed actions where the important thing is the result at a moment in the past
rows.example: By the time of his death, Thomas Edison **had invented** a number of things that changed everyday life.

blocks.text: I beat Jason at International Captain because I'd **played** it a lot with my brother. The past perfect often makes the **earlier** of two past events clear.

rows.use: Actions and situations continuing up to a moment in the past (or just before a moment in the past)
rows.example: She'd **been writing** computer games for over ten years before she finally had a hit.

rows.use: would · past habits, particularly for the distant past
rows.example: The ancient Greeks **would** rely on the power of slaves, rather than machines.

rows.use: used to · past habits and states, particularly for the distant past
rows.example: It **used to** seem strange to be able to communicate over long distances.

blocks.text: **Would** can also be used with a continuous infinitive when we are referring to a habit involving actions in progress.
blocks.note: Whenever I went to James's house, he would usually **be playing** on his computer. **Would** is not usually used to refer to past **states**.

blocks.text: Remember that **used to** is not the same as **be used to**. **Be used to** refers to a situation that is now familiar or no longer strange.
blocks.note: At first, people found it strange sending messages by mobile, but now everyone's **used to** it.

blocks.text: We use **get used to** to refer to the process of becoming familiar with a situation.
blocks.note: It's surprising how quickly people in the nineteenth century **got used to** travelling by train.
